title: La Salle-Pui Ching Programming Challenge Journal
content: My La Salle-Pui Ching Programming Challenge journal. Original: Chinese Translation: Gemini Hereinafter referred to as PLT. Registration was required just a few days before NOI. Although PLT clashed with the HKMO training team sessions, I still decided to participate in PLT. From my past experience competing in ACM, there’s a rather strange phenomenon: a three-person team shouldn’t consist entirely of top-tier players, otherwise they will underperform (who knows why). My best runs were either flying solo, or when qwertim and I teamed up with General Huang as our assistant. My absolute worst run was with Adam and ltw—both IOI team members—where we ended up dead last in HKOI. Truly hilarious. So when Matthew invited Andy and me to form a team, it was exactly what I wanted. Both of them are juniors who excel at math in our school. Plus, Andy frequently solves ad-hoc problems that stump me; Andy and I even pulled off some insane team results back at the HKOI training camp. I didn’t dare carry the older students from school, because it wouldn’t feel right if I ended up writing code the entire time, and our strengths wouldn’t complement each other. Thus, the team was formed, and we successfully became the official PCMS team. We named ourselves Polynomial Laplace Transform. Our strategy was simple. I would write code the whole time and handle all the algorithmic problems, while the two of them tackled the ad-hoc ones. The ContestBefore the contest started, Matthew introduced us to the research content of this year’s Fields Medal, and then roughly outlined a proof method for the 2D Kakeya conjecture (Note: this year’s Fields Medal was for 3D). I listened with great interest. He also said he learnt how to prove Fermat’s Last Theorem. Absolute legend. The contest began. Within the first hour, we cleared 5 warmup problems and felt in great shape. Then I noticed that many teams were solving A and C, so I had Andy think about A while I focused on C. I spent 20 minutes seriously thinking through C, while Andy was also developing some ideas for A. For C, you could just iterate through the starting points and maintain the endpoints using a set. I implemented C first, but then realized one step was flawed and I had overcomplicated things. I quickly fixed it and solved the problem. Andy came up with a brilliant position-skipping solution, which felt incredibly smart. I suggested a greedy approach, and then realized combining them worked perfectly. We took a time penalty but successfully locked it down. Next, we looked at J, which some people had solved. I realized it was a classic hashing practice problem. I initially wrote a map solution but got TLE, so I switched to hashing. I tried single-modulo hashing first but got WA, changed it to double-modulo and still got WA, only to finally discover a typo somewhere. Once fixed, it ACed, but bruh, we racked up so much time penalty. At this point, I planned to tackle F, which was a harder version of a simple problem shx had set among the SMSOIers. After thinking for 5 minutes, I saw that Adam ACed F, so it was definitely doable. I spent 20 minutes writing the code, but since it was a probability problem, it was hard to debug, so I spent another 20 minutes debugging. It felt like a terrible waste of time. Meanwhile, Andy and Matthew worked together and figured out a solution for L, which surprised me because no one had passed L yet. To be safe, I kept working on F, but it threw another TLE upon submission. I tweaked the square-root decomposition threshold, but it still TLE’d. Then we realized I couldn’t submit anything else because one of my previous submissions was stuck in Pending. At this point, there were only 5 minutes left in the contest, and we felt completely hopeless. Even when the contest ended, it was still Pending. Truly doomed. Or so we thought? It was announced that the contest would be extended by 10 minutes because the judging server was heavily lagging in the final 5 minutes, though writing new code was forbidden. Then, looking closely, that Pending submission actually passed! We were saved! In the end, we happily took RK 4. It was another classic ACM performance—most solved problems alongside the highest time penalty. The exact same thing happened at the HIT Shenzhen ACM last time. Just made the cutoff for a Gold Award, an absolute win. I became the match MVP by coding 9 problems. Honestly, if I hadn’t spent so long debugging F at the end, we could have totally cleared L and hit RK 1. But that’s on me, since my coding speed is naturally slow. Happily brought home a trophy and a medal. Took a big group photo, hung out with Adam, sang the NOI versions of “Run, Youth” and “Crossing Bridge” together, packed up, and cleared out. The End

Original: Chinese Translation: Gemini Previous post: Codeforces Training Let’s Start!Red-Blue Operations Sort first. Binary search on answer. It is easy to notice that values less than the binary search value must be operated an odd number of times. It is easy to notice that the last operations must be given according to the order. The remaining operations look like many instances of and , where the optimal choice is to subtract from the largest elements. Handle the edge case of wrong parity, and then maintain the prefix information. Traffic Lights is small, so consider DP. Since the second answer is not easy to find directly, we cannot use Dijkstra straight away. Directly sort by time , and let be the minimum cost to reach at time , or if unreachable. Perform a brute-force transition. We can guess that the time to reach has an upper bound of , which is not difficult to prove to oneself. The total complexity is , which might be tight on memory. Hyperregular Bracket Strings A brilliant problem. Playing around with small cases reveals that it essentially boils down to many constraints of valid bracket sequences with fixed lengths. We can precalculate the Catalan numbers first. The problem then reduces to finding the lengths of these constraints. Noticing that adding a constraint splits all existing segments, we can maintain this using a prefix XOR hash. Group Projects Clearly a DP problem. Sort all the people first, and the problem becomes structurally equivalent to bracket matching. Let denote that we are considering the first people, where the number of open brackets exceeds the closed brackets by , and the sum of weights of open brackets minus closed brackets is (which can be negative). We find that for each , only values of are valid, so the complexity is . Mass Change Queries There are many ways to solve this. Since there are very few colors, we only need to consider each color separately. One approach is to build a dynamically allocated segment tree for each color, making the operation equivalent to swapping segment tree nodes. However, I found that too tedious. Noticing that each value is , we can just implement a custom bitset, which runs incredibly fast! Another Exercise on Graph An excellent problem. Binary search for the answer (where only needs to take one of the edge weight values). The problem is equivalent to asking whether we can walk from to such that we traverse fewer than edges with weights . This inspires us to assign a weight of to edges and a weight of to edges , and then simply check if the shortest path from to is . Consider preprocessing. Sort all possible values of (all edge weights) from smallest to largest. Initially, all edges are assigned a weight of , and we preprocess the shortest paths using the Floyd-Warshall algorithm. Each time increases, it is equivalent to changing the weight of an edge from to . If the shortest path between and is already at this point, then all shortest paths obviously remain unchanged. Otherwise, we only need to try updating all pairs via the two potentially better paths: and . Clearly, only edges require shortest path updates. The total complexity is . Expected Destruction A math problem—I actually know how to do this one! Obviously, the maximum possible answer is the sum of the distances of all numbers to . However, if two adjacent numbers merge, the answer decreases by the distance between the merger position and . The expected value of this reduction is linear, so the problem reduces to finding the distance to when they finally merge for all pairs . Let this be . This can clearly be solved using DP. Since in each operation, either neither nor transitions, or their chances of transitioning are equal, we have . Just handle the boundary conditions. Tenzing and Tree A god-tier problem. If we root the tree at , the answer after coloring is , where is the number of black nodes in the subtree of node . We then notice that the tree can be clearly divided into two connected components: one side takes the absolute value as positive, and the other side takes it as negative (in fact, the boundary between these two blocks is the centroid of the spanning tree of the black nodes). Enumerate this boundary point as the root to build the tree; the contribution of coloring a node black becomes , so we should always pick the shallowest nodes. Finally, just take the optimal outcome among all cases. Least Cost Bracket Sequence At first glance, this is an incremental regret-based greedy problem. Treat validity as the primary objective and optimality as the secondary objective. If we can add a closing bracket currently, add it. Otherwise, choose the optimal option between adding an opening bracket and regretting a previous closing bracket by changing it to an opening bracket while picking a closing bracket. Regret operations can be maintained using a monotonic queue. But wait, why did my brute-force DP that I messed around with manage to pass anyway???? Fibonacci Additions Total brain-fade moment. The answer is then , where is the state of the column, and is the smaller value between the number of s and s in the binary bits. Let’s manipulate the formula. Ehab’s REAL Number Theory Problem Don’t be like me and think that every number has at most prime factors, or you’ll end up connecting them into a hypergraph (whoops). After removing perfect square factors, each number has at most prime factors. If there is a , we are done instantly. If it is a prime , connect an edge between and . If it is a product of primes , connect an edge between and . The original problem reduces to finding the shortest cycle (girth). Finding the shortest cycle in an unweighted undirected graph can obviously be done via BFS, i.e., running a BFS from every node and updating the cycle length. However, this takes . The first one is an interactive problem, and I don’t have any ideas at first sight. The second is obviously a DP with transition f(i)=min(f(j)+w(i, j)), which reminds me of D&C DP. So I skipped this problem. 1:10-1:30 mins: Think P1 By looking at subtasks, I quickly realized that this problem is a two-step interactive problem: find a specific pattern, and then use this pattern to quickly find information. This is by replacing the first square with all n^2 other squares, and seeing if it is equal to the minimum. In the competition, I saw Migration suddenly become very happy and instantly go to the toilet. I thought he ACed P1 (although this thought did not affect my strategy at all), but turns out he just ACed P2. After asking around for results, I found Adam 193 culver 155 carson 144 Migration 140. I feel very shocked - this was my highest rank in all HKOI competitions! And it occurred in TFT! The trainers announced all solutions in 1 nanoseconds (I didn’t listen carefully lol) and scoreboard release. Rank 3!!! (Although I believe myself to be Rank 2 if not for penalty time) However, this competition really didn’t distinguish the trainees a lot. The margins were small, and I knew that this was definitely not the end. But I did learn that I have the ability to get rank top 4, and I had more confidence in myself. Later, Soso told me to revise my strategies. Then, we went to the mall to eat some food. During the walk to the mall, 123abc showed me the Prelim answers that culver gave him right before TFT. 25pts! Nice, although it was much in my expectations. After eating, I went home with tanjianlang. I didn’t make any changes to my strategy and decided to compete in Day 2 as if I had no advantage. SundayI slept at 22:30 the night before and woke up at 07:30. After eating breakfast, I decided to revise some templates. TFT Day 2My Subtask Scoring: My Submissions: 0:00-0:45 mins: Take a look at problems, sort difficulty, brief thinking It only took me 15 mins to read and understand all the problems. Then I started thinking. For P1, I quickly discovered that I can partition the edges into tight edges and loose edges, and I can binary search on the last new tight edge for every query. Then the change is basically making all edges tight, making at most one edge from tight to loose, and making no changes to anything else. This leads to a very simple amortized solution idea, since there is at most one edge from tight to loose, the total number of edges that went from loose to tight is O(n+q). For P2, I don’t have many ideas, but Subtask 1 is very doable. I quickly found a 25pts solution, and decided to skip for now. For P3, I literally instantly solved it within 5 minutes in my mind. Using what? It’s very simple, using Bitset + Virtual Tree + Matrix + Heavy Light Decomposition + Segment Tree + Dynamic DP. O(n^2/w+n log^2 n). Yeah. I ain’t writing that bruh. For those who are interested in my toxic solution, here it is. Offline the queries, and for every color, you get a virtual tree with O(c_i) nodes, where the sum of c_i is O(n). For the nodes that are not in the virtual tree, if it is controlled by Alice, it doesn’t matter; if it is controlled by Bob, then if it has more than one child, Bob wins instantly, and we can delete this node and its subtree. The deletion can be maintained by bitset, I guess. And if it has only one child, then it doesn’t matter. For each query, we split the query into 4 operations. Now each operation is [Template] DDP (aka Dynamic Dynamic Programming). We can use Matrix + HLD + Segment Tree to maintain it. Since the sum of sizes of virtual trees is only O(n), we have solved this problem in O(n^2/w+n log^2 n). Of course, I didn’t think that this was the intended solution anyway. This time, it is not my strategy that failed, it is completely skill issue. But it’s true, and unfortunately, this problem appeared in TFT. What have I learnt from this TFT? I guess I have learnt some really important lessons: Do not immerse too deeply in one thought. Really strong OIers have a hundred different thoughts when it comes to these interactive problems, but I usually only have fewer than 2 thoughts. If it was not because I only had 1 hour left, normally I would’ve gone to the toilet. But I didn’t because it usually takes a while for the trainers to approve your toilet request, and you would have even less time left. From samples from various competitions, I have made this mistake a lot before, just to name a few: In the 2025 Guangdong MO provincial selection, I spent one hour out of 3.5 hours trying to prove a false statement in a geometry problem. In 2026 HKOI Junior, I spent 90 minutes on P4 without realizing that there was a better implementation. In 2026 CSP Senior, I debugged my code for 2 hours without avail. The reason is that I didn’t check my array declaration. In 2026 APIO, I didn’t even read P3 because I thought it was hard. Of course, it turned out to be the easiest problem in the problem set. 2026/5/24 TFT Day 2 P2. I would never forget this problem. Order the problems wisely. A really important lesson I learnt from this TFT. For example: Both Animal Migration and tosivan found the crucial D1P3 observation and dumped lots of time and energy on this problem. Turns out that this problem was the hardest in the problem set. On the other hand, I did not find the crucial observation, and so I didn’t spend time on D1P3. What does that mean? In terms of ability, my observation skills failed on P3, but I got higher marks in total on Day 1. That is luck. But if I made more observations in P3, would I have spent more time on P3? Probably yes. Would I get more marks in total? Probably no, maybe even less. What I mean is that, maybe, the smartest decision on which problem to do should be based on comparing the expected scores for each problem, not wishful thinking. And now on Day 2, I made the same mistake. If I hadn’t spent about 1 hour wasting time on P1’s case analysis, I would have definitely achieved a high score in P2. But why did I spend so much time on P1? It was probably because of confidence in my tree abilities. And later, it was because of my unwillingness to only get 23pts when I wrote a near-full solution. The instant I saw 2 tree problems in the problem set, I told myself that I probably have the ability to AC at least one problem. Do not ignore non-batch problems. Spend more time on it. Unlike batch problems that can be easily trained to be good at, non-batch problems need lots of observation and ideas, even if they are not good or sufficient to solve the problem. And as I have said, I usually only have fewer than 2 ideas in interactive problems. I really need to do more non-batch problems. If TFT only had the four batch problems, you can find that I rank second in the leaderboard (because Adam trained even more than me on batch problems). Sometimes, a non-batch problem’s scores are correlated with the time spent on it. Such as both D1P1 and D2P2. It is really not a good strategy to not spend much time on non-batch problems. 最後的最後，愿後來者，警鐘長鳴！ - tanjianlang AfterwordsShould I be happy or sad? Given a directed weighted graph that may contain negative edge weights, find the shortest path from to . Aside from using SPFA which takes , we can consider another approach. Consider assigning a fixed potential to each node, and transforming each original edge into . The potentials must satisfy for every edge. For any path from to , the new total length becomes: In other words, it exceeds the original length by exactly a constant . We can simply run Dijkstra’s algorithm to find the shortest path, and then subtract this constant. So how do we find these potentials? You will notice that is exactly a system of difference constraints, which can be solved as follows: Construct a super source based on the original graph, and connect a directed edge with weight from to every other node. Run SPFA starting from , and then set the potential to be the shortest distance from to . By the triangle inequality, holds trivially. Solution : Since it is a DAG, the potentials are already given to you, so running SPFA is unnecessary. The potential can be set as , where represents the topological order of . Then, just run Dijkstra, which takes . Johnson’s Algorithm(A faster all-pairs shortest path algorithm on sparse graphs) Problem: Given a weighted graph (which may contain negative edge weights), find the all-pairs shortest paths. Time limit: 2s. Solution: Floyd’s algorithm will TLE. However, we could run Dijkstra from each node, which takes . Wait, Dijkstra does not support negative edge weights. Then we could use SPFA from each node, which takes in the worst case, making it even slower. Instead, we can use the potential method. First, run SPFA once to transform all edge weights, and then run Dijkstra from each node. The total time complexity is . Primal-Dual Algorithm(A faster minimum-cost maximum-flow algorithm) Problem: Min-Cost Max-Flow (MCMF). Solution: Consider how to optimize the brute-force approach: it performs at most augmentations, with each augmentation taking using a shortest path algorithm. Let’s try to optimize it to per augmentation. At the very beginning, we use SPFA to calculate the shortest paths from the source to all other nodes on the original graph, which serves as the initial potential . This transforms all initial edge weights into non-negative numbers, allowing us to perform augmentations using Dijkstra. However, a problem arises: after an augmentation, residual edges are created, and their weights are negative. Does this mean we have to run SPFA all over again? Actually, we don’t. We can directly update the potential by adding the shortest distance from the source to that node: . We can prove that this updated potential satisfies the required condition. First, for any edge that was augmented, it must satisfy . The weight of its residual edge was originally , and now it becomes , which is non-negative. Second, for any original edge in the graph, the new edge weight is , which is also clearly non-negative. Thus, the condition holds. The total complexity is . In particular, if the initial graph has no negative edge weights, the first potential calculation can also use Dijkstra, reducing the complexity to . Create a super sink , and add two edges and with weights of . Set the capacity of each edge to and the cost to its edge weight. Then run MCMF with as the source and as the sink. Using the Primal-Dual algorithm, the complexity is . In practice, you do not need to fully implement the Primal-Dual algorithm; you can just simulate Dijkstra twice. Using the mysterious Orlin’s Algorithm, it can be optimized to strongly polynomial time . The problem states that certain adjacent positions can be swapped. It is easy to see that within these large swappable “blocks” (i.e., an interval such that ), the characters can be sorted arbitrarily. That is, we can achieve any permutation of these characters through a finite number of adjacent swaps. Therefore, we can first pre-process and identify these “blocks.” Then, we naturally iterate from left to right. If the characters match, we just match them. If they do not match, we check whether there is a character within the same block that can be brought to the current position to form a match. If such a character exists, we perform a swap; otherwise, we just give up on this position, meaning it cannot be matched. So, how do we maintain the characters available for matching within a block? We can notice that during the iteration, the position of the first available character that can form a match is monotonically non-decreasing (because once a swap is made, the next available position must be strictly after it).
